subject: Sizing guidance: model-aware KV allocation & quantization for Fenwick
messages:
From: Priyom Das <priyom_das@redwood.com>
To: Joe Turner <joe@fenwick.ai>
Cc: Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.com>, Lauren Bishop <lauren_bishop@redwood.com>
Date: Thu, 30 Aug 2028 10:12:00 -0700
Subject: Sizing guidance: model-aware KV allocation & quantization for Fenwick

Joe — thanks again for the call this morning. Per our conversation, attaching a concise sizing note so your infra/procurement teams can evaluate committed-pool options. See the short bullets below; I also attached a cleaned model profile you sent (fenwick_model_profile.csv) and a first-pass draft of the reserved-pool proposal.

Top-line asks from our side:
- Confirm target models you plan to serve (you mentioned a tuned 35B and a fine-tuned 70B variant).
- Expected P99 latency target and steady-state QPS (we used 8 rps for the sample compute below).
- Typical generation lengths and max context (you mentioned 12k working set with occasional 32k bursts).

Quick recommendations summary (full detail below):
1) Favor 80GB-class GPUs for the reserved pool to give headroom for KV cache spikes (32k bursts) and mixed-precision variants.
2) Ship a mixed-precision strategy in the contract: default nf4/int8 for online traffic, fallback to fp16 for eval/rare cases.
3) Reserve a small burst pool of CPU-offload hosts for long-context (>24k) archive sessions to avoid overprovisioning GPU capacity.

Sizing rationale and numbers (estimates for planning):
- Model footprint: a 35B model quantized to 4-bit weights (nf4) + fp16 activations typically consumes ~10–18 GB of GPU-resident weight memory (variability depends on tokenizer and adapter layers). A 70B baseline (also nf4) sits in the ~20–32 GB range for weights.
- KV cache: the dominant variable for long contexts. For the 35B variant we estimate per-token KV state in the low hundreds of bytes; for planning, assume ~0.5–0.8 KB/token. That implies:
  - 12k context -> ~6–10 GB KV per concurrent request (depending on value/key precision and layer counts).
  - 32k context burst -> ~16–26 GB KV per request.
- Activation / workspace: add ~8–16 GB depending on batch/concurrent streams and generation length.

Aggregate per-instance working memory (rounded planning numbers):
- 35B nf4 (serving path) with 12k context, single concurrent session: ~30–40 GB (weights + KV + activations).
- 70B nf4 with 12k context: ~45–60 GB.
- 70B with 32k burst: plan for 70–95 GB headroom if you want single-GPU single-request handling at peak context without offload.

Implication: to comfortably support your stated traffic profile and 32k burst windows, 80GB GPUs (H100 80GB or A100 80GB class) are the recommended baseline for reserved capacity. If you standardize on 48GB cards, expect to need 1.5–2x more GPUs plus active KV offload or model-slicing logic.

Quantization tradeoffs and operational notes:
- nf4/int4 (production path): reduces GPU parameter memory by ~2–4x vs fp16, lowers peak GPU requirement and increases per-GPU concurrency. NF4 is our recommended production default for tuned models; it preserves generation quality and reduces memory pressure.
- int8 path: a middle ground providing slightly higher fidelity for small, sensitive prompts with modest memory savings.
- fp16 path: retains highest fidelity and is useful for short A/B evals, but costs 2–3x more GPU memory — keep as a fallback.

Operational strategies to reduce committed footprint:
- Prefix/KV caching: cache commonly repeated prefixes and reuse KV segments; this reduces effective KV per request for many of your workflows (document summarization/QA patterns).
- Dynamic routing: route short, latency-critical requests to a lower-precision 35B pool and long-context archival sessions to a separate, slower pool or CPU-offload nodes.
- Canary policies: start a small reserved pool of 6–8 80GB GPUs and grow to the steady-state number after 2–3 weeks of traffic profiling.

Sample reserved-pool plan (assumptions: 8 rps steady-state, average gen 512 tokens, 10% concurrent long-context sessions):
- Baseline pool: 8 x H100-80GB (handles primary throughput for nf4 35B + pooling headroom).
- Long-context buffer: 4 x H100-80GB thin pool (for 70B serving and 32k bursts), backed by autoscale / burst credits.
- CPU-offload set: 6 x large CPU nodes for archival/very long contexts and for running occasional fp16-only evals.

Next steps: I put together a short two-sheet we can share with procurement and infra (attached). If that aligns, Marcus and I can model monthly committed costs versus a hybrid reserved+burst commit and produce a comparison using your QPS and expected growth.

Thanks — happy to walk through the numbers with your ops folks.

— Priyom

From: Joe Turner <joe@fenwick.ai>

Subject: Re: Sizing guidance: model-aware KV allocation & quantization for Fenwick

Priyom — thanks for the writeup. A couple quick clarifications from our infra team: we currently intend to push the tuned 70B for most generation tasks (higher quality), but we expect ~30% of traffic to hit a distilled 13B during peak hours for lower-cost front-line routing. Are your KV estimates per full model or per hidden-size variant? Also, can you call out the expected impact on latency for nf4 vs fp16 for generation?

— Joe
VP, ML Engineering, Fenwick Therapeutics
joe@fenwick.ai

-----Reply & Clarification-----
From: Priyom Das <priyom_das@redwood.com>
To: Joe Turner <joe@fenwick.ai>
Cc: Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.com>, Lauren Bishop <lauren_bishop@redwood.com>
Date: Thu, 30 Aug 2028 14:38:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Sizing guidance: model-aware KV allocation & quantization for Fenwick

Joe — great questions. Short answers:
- KV sizing references the full model architecture in the profile you provided; smaller variants (13B) drop KV proportionally (roughly linear with hidden size and number of layers), so for planning you can assume ~40–50% of the 35B KV for a 13B distilled model.
- Latency impact: nf4/int4 typically adds negligible decode-time overhead vs fp16 (our inference kernels are optimized for these quant formats). In practice you should expect <5–10% difference for end-to-end generation latency at comparable batch sizes. fp16 can sometimes be faster on older kernels if you avoid quant-dequant overhead, but the memory headroom tradeoff usually favors nf4 in production.

Attached I added a very short per-variant table in the Drive link listing projected per-request memory buckets (weights/KV/activations) for 13B / 35B / 70B under nf4 and fp16. I also included a conservative headroom multiplier (x1.3) to cover scheduling jitter and multi-tenant noise.

If you want, Marcus and I can put numbers into your cost model and show committed vs burst economics — recommend a 3-month pilot with 8 reserved 80GB GPUs and a 30% burst pool to validate assumptions.

— Priyom

-----Forwarded Note-----
From: Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.com>
To: Joe Turner <joe@fenwick.ai>
Cc: Priyom Das <priyom_das@redwood.com>, Lauren Bishop <lauren_bishop@redwood.com>
Date: Fri, 31 Aug 2028 16:05:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Sizing guidance: model-aware KV allocation & quantization for Fenwick

Joe / team — looping in a short ops checklist we use during provisioning so procurement has items to track with vendors:
1) Confirm GPU SKU availability and expected lead times in target region (we recommend H100-80GB or equivalent).
2) Include language for dynamic scaling credits in the contract (ability to allocate burst GPUs on demand).
3) Audit logging: we will need access to telemetry hooks (latency/cost per token) to tune pooling and quantization thresholds.
4) Maintenance windows: schedule low-traffic windows for model updates and quantization changes to avoid SLA blips.

Priyom — I put a rough cost delta appendix in the Drive doc showing the difference between deploying primarily on 80GB NF4 vs a mixed 48GB+CPU offload approach so Joe's team can see the TCO tradeoffs.

Joe — happy to sync with your procurement lead next week; suggest Tue or Wed afternoon PT.

— Marcus Lin
Head of Capacity Planning, Redwood Inference
